title: Key-Value Store
seoTitle: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store Like DynamoDB
description: Design a durable distributed key-value store — partitioning with consistent hashing, replication, tunable quorums, conflict resolution, and failure handling.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Key-Value Store?
blocks.text: A distributed key-value store saves values under keys across many machines — `put(key, value)` and `get(key)` — and keeps working when machines fail. Amazon's Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak are classic examples.

items: Clients should be able to `put(key, value)` and `get(key)`.
Data must persist durably across restarts.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Highly available — reads and writes keep working when nodes or a data center fail.
Low latency (single-digit milliseconds at p99) for values up to ~1MB.
Horizontally scalable to petabytes and millions of requests per second.
Tunable consistency: callers can choose stronger or faster per request.
**Key / Value**: the data, plus a version (vector clock or timestamp).
**Node**: a storage server owning parts of the key space.
**Partition**: a range of the hash ring with its replicas.

blocks.text: 1) Clients should be able to put and get keys

Keys are hashed onto a **consistent hash ring**. Each key is stored on the first N nodes clockwise from its position (N = replication factor, typically 3). Any node can act as **coordinator**: it receives the request, forwards it to the key's replicas, and waits for enough acknowledgements.

blocks.caption: Replicated writes on a hash ring

blocks.text: Each node writes to an append-only **commit log** first, then into an in-memory table (memtable) that is periodically flushed to immutable sorted files (SSTables) — an LSM tree. Background compaction merges files and drops deleted (tombstoned) keys.
3) Clients should be able to delete keys
Deletes write a **tombstone** with a version rather than removing data immediately, so replicas that missed the delete don't resurrect the old value during repair.
1) How do we choose between consistency and availability?

approach.text: One replica per partition is the leader and orders all writes; followers copy them.

challenges.text: Strong consistency per key, but writes stall during leader failover.

approach.text: Write to all N replicas and wait for W acks; read from R replicas and return the newest version. If **R + W > N**, every read overlaps at least one replica with the latest write. Callers tune per request: `W=1` for fast writes, `R=W=QUORUM` for stronger reads.

challenges.text: Concurrent writes to the same key can conflict; we need versioning and conflict resolution (below).

blocks.text: 2) How do we resolve conflicting writes?

approach.text: Keep the value with the latest timestamp.

challenges.text: Clock skew can silently drop a newer write.

approach.text: Use hybrid logical timestamps so ordering respects causality within bounded skew. Simple and good enough for most data.

challenges.text: Truly concurrent writes still lose one side.

approach.text: Each value carries a vector clock. If one version descends from another, keep the newer; if they're concurrent, return both "siblings" to the client to merge (e.g. union of shopping-cart items).

challenges.text: Pushes merge logic to clients and clocks must be pruned.

blocks.text: 3) How do we handle node failures?

items: **Hinted handoff**: if a replica is down, another node accepts the write with a "hint" and forwards it when the replica returns.
**Read repair**: when a read sees stale replicas, the coordinator writes the newest version back to them.
**Anti-entropy**: replicas periodically compare **Merkle trees** of their key ranges and sync only the branches that differ.
**Gossip**: nodes exchange membership and health state so everyone learns about failures.

quiz.question: With N=3 replicas, which setting guarantees reads see the latest acknowledged write?
quiz.explanation: R + W > N ensures read and write sets overlap.

quiz.question: Why are deletes written as tombstones?
options: So replicas that missed the delete don't resurrect old data
quiz.explanation: Tombstones carry a version that wins over the stale value during repair.

quiz.question: What is hinted handoff?
options: Another node temporarily accepts writes for a down replica and forwards them later
quiz.explanation: It keeps writes available during short outages.

quiz.question: What do Merkle trees enable between replicas?
options: Efficiently finding and syncing only the key ranges that differ
quiz.explanation: Comparing hashes top-down avoids transferring the whole dataset.
